newsitem.title: USA: Stocks jump, rates drop after inflation data.
newsitem.headline: Stocks jump, rates drop after inflation data.

text.p: Stocks powered higher Thursday on the back of a tame wholesale price report that triggered a rally in the bond market and sent interest rates lower.
Just after 1:15 p.m. EST, the Dow Jones industrial average rose 62.72 points to 6,612.20, above the record of close of 6,600.66 set on Tuesday.
In the broader market, advancing issues beat declines by a 14-9 margin on active volume of 314 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The Nasdaq composite index added 4.13 to 1,324.48. The American Stock Exchange index gained 3.02 at 579.74.

Stocks got an early boost from the government's report that the Producer Price Index rose 0.5 percent in December -- the biggest increase in 1996 -- but the so-called core rate, excluding volatile food and energy prices, rose a scant 0.1 percent.
"The PPI core rate was in line, and that gave bonds a lift," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury rose 27/32, lowering its yield 6.77 percent from 6.84 percent on Wednesday. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
The report allayed fears that a pickup in economic growth might spark a rise in the rate of inflation.
The bond market rally lifted a weight off the stock market, which sold off sharply late on Wednesday under the pressure of rising rates in the bond market.
Analysts said that the Labour Department's report, while positive, also reinforced some concerns for financial markets.

"Several things are happening in tandem to pressure stocks," said Peggy Farley, chief executive at Amas Securities. "One is that oil prices are high and we're still seeing cold weather across Europe and much of the U.S."
Indeed, a sharp increase in energy prices was the main reason for the rise in the Labour Department's Producer Price Index.
Analysts have voiced concern about energy prices, but Chicago Federal Reserve President Michael Moskow said that he was not alarmed by the increase yet.
"If energy starts to spill over into the cost of goods and services, then it becomes a concern," Moskow said after a speech to a business group in Chicago. "But we haven't seen that yet."
Crude oil for February delivery hovered near $26.60 a barrel on the New York Mercantile Exchange, nearing its six-year peak of $26.80 hit in late December.
Oil company shares rose sharply. Texaco Inc. jumped 3-1/8 to 105-1/8 and Exxon Corp. gained 2-1/8 to 101-5/8. Both stocks are components of the 30-stock Dow index.

Raytheon Co. fell 1-3/4 to 47 after the Wall Street Journal reported that the company had bid $9 billion for the defence assets of Hughes Electronics Corp. The report also said Northrop Grumman Corp. had submitted an even higher bid for the business.
Raytheon and Hughes parent General Motors Corp. both declined to comment on the report. Hughes shares rose 1-3/4 to 62-7/8 and GM shares edged up 1/8 to 59-1/4.
